terms.meaning: An animal whose adult body has three parts and six legs.
terms.example: An ant has six legs and a body in three parts, so she is an insect. A spider has eight legs, so she is not.
terms.art: An ant drawn large from the side, with six legs and three body parts marked.

terms.meaning: The middle part of an insect's body, where the six legs and the wings join.
terms.example: On a housefly, both wings and all six legs join the thorax.
terms.art: A housefly with the middle part coloured and the legs and wings joined to it.

terms.meaning: The back part of an insect's body. It holds the stomach and, in females, the eggs.
terms.example: A grasshopper's abdomen moves in and out when she breathes.
terms.art: A grasshopper with the back part coloured.

terms.meaning: The two jointed feelers on an insect's head. They smell, taste, touch and feel the air.
terms.example: An ant taps her antennae on the ground to follow a smell trail.
terms.art: An ant with two bent antennae touching a line of scent on the ground.

terms.meaning: A hard cover on the outside of an animal's body that does the job of a skeleton.
terms.example: The brown empty shell stuck to a tree trunk after the rains is a cicada's old exoskeleton.
terms.art: An empty brown cicada skin clinging to a tree trunk.

terms.meaning: The tough, light material that an insect's exoskeleton is made of.
terms.example: A beetle's wing covers are made of chitin. They are light and very strong.
terms.art: A beetle with the hard wing covers lifted, showing the soft wings below.

terms.meaning: Shedding the old exoskeleton so that a bigger one can harden.
terms.example: A silkworm moults four times before she spins her cocoon.
terms.art: A silkworm climbing out of a split old skin, with a soft new skin beneath.

terms.meaning: An animal with jointed legs and an exoskeleton. Insects, spiders, centipedes and prawns are all arthropods.
terms.example: A prawn, a spider and a beetle are all arthropods, though only the beetle is an insect.
terms.art: A beetle, a spider and a prawn side by side with their jointed legs marked.

terms.meaning: A stand with three legs. Three legs always rest steadily on a flat surface.
terms.example: A camera stand has three legs and never rocks. An ant walks on two tripods in turn.
terms.art: A camera on a tripod beside an ant walking, with three of her legs lit up.

terms.meaning: A smell that an animal gives off as a message to others of her own kind.
terms.example: A female silk moth gives off a pheromone that a male can sense from far away.
terms.art: A female moth on a branch with a curl of scent drifting to a male moth far away.

terms.meaning: An eye made of many tiny lenses packed together, each looking in a slightly different direction.
terms.example: A dragonfly has up to about 30,000 lenses in each compound eye.
terms.art: A close-up of a dragonfly's head with two large eyes in a honeycomb pattern.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that bees can see and our eyes cannot.
terms.example: A flower that looks plain yellow to you may have ultraviolet lines that a bee sees pointing to the nectar.
terms.art: A yellow flower shown twice, plain on one side and with dark guiding lines on the other.

terms.meaning: A small breathing hole along the side of an insect's body.
terms.example: A row of small dots along a caterpillar's side are her spiracles.
terms.art: A green caterpillar from the side, with a row of small dots along her body.

terms.meaning: The thin air tubes inside an insect that carry air from the spiracles to every part of the body.
terms.example: A grasshopper's tracheae branch again and again, until air reaches every muscle.
terms.art: A cut-away grasshopper showing fine branching tubes from side holes.

terms.meaning: The mark or the remains of a living being from long ago, kept in rock.
terms.example: A fossil dragonfly-like insect found in rock has wings about 70 centimetres across, much wider than any dragonfly alive.
terms.art: A dark outline of a giant insect wing pressed into a grey rock.

terms.meaning: The young stage of an insect who grows up in four stages. She looks nothing like the adult.
terms.example: A silkworm is the larva of the silk moth, and a maggot is the larva of a fly.
terms.art: A silkworm on a mulberry leaf and a maggot, each labelled larva.

terms.meaning: The stage in which a larva's body is rebuilt into the adult's body.
terms.example: A silkworm becomes a pupa inside her cocoon, and a moth comes out about two weeks later.
terms.art: A cocoon cut open to show a brown pupa inside.

terms.meaning: A case of thread that a larva spins around herself before she becomes a pupa.
terms.example: A silkworm spins her cocoon from one thread that can be several hundred metres long.
terms.art: A white oval cocoon hanging on a twig.

terms.meaning: Growing up in four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
terms.example: A butterfly, a beetle, a fly and a mosquito all grow up in four stages.
terms.art: Four pictures in a row: egg, caterpillar, pupa, butterfly.

terms.meaning: The young stage of an insect who grows up in three stages. She looks like a small adult with no working wings.
terms.example: A grasshopper nymph looks like a small grasshopper with tiny wing buds.
terms.art: A grasshopper nymph beside an adult, with wing buds and wings marked.

terms.meaning: Growing up in three stages: egg, nymph and adult.
terms.example: Grasshoppers, cockroaches, crickets and dragonflies all grow up in three stages.
terms.art: Three pictures in a row: egg, nymph, adult grasshopper.

terms.meaning: A fine powder that a flower makes. It must reach another flower of the same kind to make seeds.
terms.example: A bee comes away from a mustard flower with yellow dust on her body.
terms.art: A bee on a mustard flower with yellow dust on her legs and back.

terms.meaning: The moving of pollen from one flower to another flower of the same kind, so that seeds and fruits can grow.
terms.example: A fly moving pollen between mango flowers makes the fruit grow.
terms.art: A fly moving from one mango flower to the next, with dust on her legs.

terms.meaning: An animal who carries pollen from flower to flower.
terms.example: A bee, a fly, a butterfly and a beetle can all be pollinators.
terms.art: A bee, a fly and a butterfly each visiting a flower.

terms.meaning: The sweet drink that a flower makes to pay visitors.
terms.example: A bee pushes into a flower to drink nectar and gets dusted with pollen on the way.
terms.art: A bee with her tongue in a flower, with a drop of nectar shining.

terms.meaning: In a honeybee family, the one large bee who lays all the eggs.
terms.example: A honeybee queen is the mother of every worker in her hive.
terms.art: A large queen bee on a comb with workers around her.

terms.meaning: In a honeybee family, a female bee who builds the comb, feeds the young, guards the door and collects food.
terms.example: Every worker honeybee is a daughter of the queen.
terms.art: A worker bee carrying pollen on her back legs.

terms.meaning: A male honeybee. His one job is to mate with a new queen.
terms.example: A drone does not collect food or guard the hive.
terms.art: A drone bee with big eyes beside a worker.

terms.meaning: The wall of six-sided wax cells that honeybees build to hold eggs, honey and pollen.
terms.example: The Indian rock bee hangs one huge comb from a cliff or a tall tree.
terms.art: A piece of honeycomb with six-sided cells, some holding honey and some holding bee young.

terms.meaning: A very large crowd of insects who move together. A honeybee swarm is a crowd of bees looking for a new home.
terms.example: A locust swarm can cover many square kilometres of sky.
terms.art: A cloud of locusts over a field, and a hanging clump of honeybees on a branch.

terms.meaning: A movement a honeybee makes on the comb to show her sisters the direction and distance of flowers.
terms.example: A longer waggle means flowers farther away, and the direction shows the way compared with the Sun.
terms.art: A bee on a comb walking a straight line, waggling, with sisters watching.

terms.meaning: A thread that a silkworm makes to spin her cocoon.
terms.example: A silk sari is made of the thread of thousands of cocoons.
terms.art: A silk sari border beside a cocoon and a thread.

terms.meaning: Rearing silk moths for their thread.
terms.example: In Karnataka, families grow mulberry trees to feed silkworms for their thread.
terms.art: A tray of silkworms eating mulberry leaves in a rearing room.

terms.meaning: A small, soft insect who sucks the juice of a plant.
terms.example: Look under a rose leaf and you may see a crowd of green aphids.
terms.art: A cluster of green aphids on a rose stem.

terms.meaning: An animal who hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A ladybird is a predator of aphids, and a dragonfly is a predator of mosquitoes.
terms.art: A ladybird eating an aphid on a leaf.

terms.meaning: Protecting a crop by helping the animals who hunt the insects who eat it.
terms.example: In 2010, scientists released a tiny wasp that hunts the papaya mealybug, and the fields recovered.
terms.art: A tiny wasp laying her egg in a mealybug on a papaya leaf.

terms.meaning: A living being who breaks down dead plants, dead animals and dung so that what they are made of returns to the soil.
terms.example: A dung beetle buries a ball of dung, and the soil gets the food.
terms.art: A dung beetle rolling a ball of dung along a path.

terms.meaning: An animal who carries a germ from one body to another.
terms.example: A mosquito who carries the malaria germ from one person to another is a vector.
terms.art: A mosquito biting an arm, with a tiny germ drawn inside her.

terms.meaning: A living being who lives in or on another one and takes food from her.
terms.example: The tiny living beings that cause malaria are parasites that live in a mosquito's stomach wall and in a person's blood.
terms.art: A mosquito cut open to show tiny parasites in her stomach wall.

terms.meaning: A word people use for an insect who eats or spoils something they want, or carries illness. It describes what an insect is doing in one place.
terms.example: Ants in the sugar tin are called pests. The same ants carrying away a dead moth are doing a helpful job.
terms.art: Ants at a sugar tin on one side, and ants carrying a dead moth on the other.

terms.meaning: A poison made to kill animals who damage crops.
terms.example: A spray meant for aphids can also kill ladybirds and bees.
terms.art: A farmer's spray drifting over a leaf with an aphid, a ladybird and a bee.

terms.meaning: A fall in numbers over time.
terms.example: Fewer fireflies in a street than there were years ago would be a decline, if counted the same way each year.
terms.art: A line on a graph sloping down over many years.

games.players: 1 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough, and it also works alone.
games.context: In this card game you collect all the stages of an insect's life, from egg to adult. You learn which insects grow up in four stages and which in three.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: one row for each player
items: Player name. Cards laid down, one point for each card.
Bonus points, one for each set where you said how the young look different from the adult.

rules: Shuffle the 28 cards. With two players, deal 7 cards each. With three or four players, deal 5 each. Put the rest face down as the draw pile.
On your turn, ask any player for one stage card. Name the insect and the stage. For example: 'Do you have the pupa of the ladybird?' You may ask only for an insect whose card you already hold.

If the player has the card, they hand it over and you ask again. If not, they say 'Go and grow!' and you take the top card of the draw pile. If it is the card you asked for, show it and ask again. If not, your turn ends.

When you hold every stage of one insect, lay the cards in life order on the table and read the back of each aloud. That is 4 cards for the silk moth, ladybird, mosquito and dung beetle, and 3 cards for the grasshopper, dragonfly, cockroach and cricket. Score 1 point for each card.

Take 1 bonus point if you can say how the young stage looks different from the adult. The silk moth's young is a worm and the adult has wings. The grasshopper's young looks like the adult, only smaller.
If you have no cards in your hand on your turn, draw 3 cards from the pile, or all that are left.
The game ends when all eight insects have been laid down. The player with the most points wins. If you tie, share the win.
Playing alone: spread all 28 cards face up. Sort them into the eight insects and put each set in life order. Time yourself, and try to beat your time.

flow.do: Show your child one four-stage set and one three-stage set, and read out the backs. Ask what is different.
flow.say: Some insects grow up in four stages, with a pupa. Others grow in three stages, with no pupa. In this game you collect them all.
flow.kid: Look at the silk moth and the grasshopper. How many stages does each have?
flow.parent: Four-stage growth is called complete metamorphosis. Three-stage growth is called incomplete metamorphosis. Both words are in the terms, and you do not need them to play.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. Take turns to ask for cards. Read the back of each card aloud when a set is laid down.
flow.say: Which insect do you want next? Which stage are you missing?
flow.kid: Ask for a card. Collect all the stages of one insect.
flow.parent: With two players, the draw pile starts with 14 cards. Everyone can always move, because a player with an empty hand draws 3 cards. Let your child ask first if you are playing a younger child.

flow.do: When the game ends, ask which insects grow up in three stages and which in four. Ask where each young one lives.
flow.say: Which young ones live in water? Which ones are nothing like their parents?
flow.kid: Which insects grow up in three stages? Which in four?
flow.think: A caterpillar and a butterfly eat different foods. What could be good about that for the whole family?

ask.q: Which insects in the game live in water when they are young?

Mosquito wrigglers and dragonfly nymphs.

games.title: Friend, Foe or Both? A game of arguing both sides
games.players: 1 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough, and it also works alone.
games.context: In this game you read about an insect in one place and call her friend, foe or both. Then you find a place where the same insect would get the opposite name.

setup.art: A pile of 14 scene cards face down on a table, with a score sheet and a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 14 cards and shuffle them into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while a parent listens.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and say friend, foe or both.

setup.art: A child thinking with a finger on the chin, with a different drawing of the same insect floating in a thought bubble.
setup.caption: 3. Find a place where the same insect would get the opposite name.

printables.title: 14 scene cards, to cut out, with the other side of the story on the back

items.f: Ants walk into the sugar tin in your kitchen.
items.b: In the kitchen, a foe to your sugar. On a balcony, the same ants carry away a dead moth and loosen the soil. Same ants, two places.

items.f: A caterpillar eats holes in a curry-leaf plant.
items.b: A foe to the leaves. Three weeks later the same insect is a butterfly who carries pollen. The name changes with what she is doing.

items.f: Termites chew the wooden frame of a door.
items.b: A foe to the door. In a forest, the same termites turn fallen wood back into soil.

items.f: A lone desert locust sits in the grass at the edge of a field.
items.b: Alone, she harms nobody. In a crowded swarm, the same animal changes colour and behaviour, and a swarm can eat in a day what thousands of people eat.

items.f: A mosquito bites you at night.
items.b: A foe to you, because some carry malaria or dengue. Her young feed fish and dragonfly nymphs, and male mosquitoes drink nectar and pollinate some flowers.

items.f: A ladybird sits on a rose covered with aphids.
items.b: A friend to the rose, because she eats the aphids. Not every ladybird hunts. One kind with 28 spots eats brinjal leaves instead.

items.f: A wasp hovers over a picnic.
items.b: A nuisance at the picnic. All summer, the same wasp hunts caterpillars to feed her young.

items.f: Flies crowd onto the flowers of a mango tree.
items.b: Many people shoo them away. Flies are the main pollinators of mango, so no flies could mean few mangoes.

items.f: Dung beetles roll a ball of dung along a village path.
items.b: A messy sight, and the dung is buried, which feeds the soil. Australia's pastures were covered in cow pats until the right dung beetles were brought in.

items.f: A silkworm spins her cocoon on a rearing tray.
items.b: A friend to the weaver's family who depends on the thread. When the cocoon is heated for the thread, the pupa inside dies. Eri silk lets the moth leave. Who should decide?

items.f: Maggots work on a dead animal in a field.
items.b: Unpleasant to look at, and they are the clean-up crew. Some hospitals use clean maggots to clear dead tissue from wounds.

items.f: A cockroach walks across the kitchen floor at night.
items.b: A foe in the kitchen, because she can carry germs on her feet. In a forest, the same kind of insect helps to break down fallen leaves.

items.f: Bees have built a comb under the water tank on your roof.
items.b: Some people want the bees gone because they might sting. Others say rock bees pollinate the whole neighbourhood. People who know bees can move a comb safely, so nobody should poke at it.

items.f: A dragonfly lands on a reed beside a pond.
items.b: A friend to people, because she eats mosquitoes. She also eats flies and small butterflies. So who is her friend, and who is her foe?

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: one column for each player
items: Points for each reason given, one for each.
Points for each opposite place found, two for each.
Points for each extra view added by another player, one for each.

rules: Shuffle the 14 cards into a pile, face down. One player is the speaker and takes the top card. Read the front aloud, but do not read the back yet.
The speaker says 'friend', 'foe' or 'both' for the insect in this place, and gives one reason. Score 1 point for the reason.
Then the speaker must name a different place or a different time where the same insect would get the opposite name. Score 2 points for a place that makes sense to the others.
If the speaker cannot find a place, any other player may offer one. That player scores 2 points.
Any other player may add a view that no one has said yet, such as the plant's side, the insect's side or the farmer's side. Score 1 point for each new view.
Now read the back of the card aloud. Talk about whether you agree.
Pass the pile to the next player. The game ends when all 14 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If you tie, share the win.
No one may say 'pest' or 'helper' without saying where and when the insect is doing the thing.
Playing alone: read a card, say your answer, then read the back. Score 1 point for each idea on the back that you said before reading it. Play the pile twice and see if your score goes up.

flow.do: Read out the first card to your child. Say friend, foe or both, and give a reason. Then ask your child to find a place where the same insect would get the other name.
flow.say: We call an insect a friend or a foe by where she is and what she is doing. Let us try it with a card.
flow.kid: Listen to the first card. Say friend, foe or both. Say why.
flow.parent: Model the answer once in a short sentence. Children often say 'foe' for stinging or biting insects and 'friend' for pretty ones. Ask them to give the reason, not only the word.

flow.do: Play through the cards by the rules. Keep score on the sheet.
flow.say: What is the insect doing? Where is she? Where would she get a different name?
flow.kid: Read a card. Say friend, foe or both. Find a place where she would get the other name.
flow.parent: There is no wrong word, only a better or weaker reason. When someone says 'foe', ask what the insect would be doing in a forest or on a flower. A real discussion matters more than the points.

flow.do: When the game ends, ask which insect was the hardest to name, and why.
flow.say: Which insect was the hardest? Did you change your mind about anyone?
flow.kid: Which insect was hardest to name? Did you change your mind about anyone?
flow.think: If the name changes with the place, where does the 'friend' or 'foe' live: in the insect or in us?

experiments.title: The Ant Café: what do your ants choose, and how fast does the news spread?
experiments.question: Four small foods sit in a row beside an ant trail: sugar water, salt water, plain water and an oily crumb. Which one do the ants visit most, and how quickly do more ants come once one ant has found the best food?
experiments.predict: Before you set anything out, guess which food will get the most ants and which will get the fewest. Say why you think so. Then guess how many minutes the first ant will take to find the best one.
experiments.fair_test: The four foods sit on four identical squares of tissue, in one row, each the same distance from the trail. Only the food changes. Each food is counted every 2 minutes for 10 minutes. Then the row is reversed and the foods are counted for 10 minutes more, because ants may simply like the square nearest to where they arrive. A food that wins in both rounds is a real winner.

materials.item: a line of ants, on a kitchen floor, a window sill or a balcony
4 small katoris or cups
sugar, salt and a teaspoon
kitchen tissue cut into 4 squares of about 2 centimetres
a pinch of a fried snack such as sev or mixture, crushed
a card or a flat piece of cardboard about the size of a postcard
paper tape or sticky tape
a phone or clock with a timer
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Do not touch the ants, because some kinds bite. Look from a hand's length away. Wash your hands with soap afterwards. Wipe up every drop of sugar water at the end, so that no trail leads into the kitchen.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for both rounds. Add up each food's ants across the two rounds and draw four bars, one for each food. Write the minute when the first ant touched any square, and the minute when one square first held 5 ants. Then write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment you set out four foods for the ants near your home and count who comes to each one. You find out what your ants choose, and how fast one ant's discovery turns into a crowd.

setup.art: A child sitting on a kitchen floor, an arm's length from a line of ants at the foot of a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Find a line of ants and sit an arm's length back.

setup.art: A card with four tissue squares in a row, marked A, B, C and D, and two katoris beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Make the four foods and put them on tissue squares in a row.

setup.art: The card taped to the floor beside the ant line, with a phone timer beside the card.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the card down so every square is the same distance from the trail.

setup.art: A hand counting ants on four tissue squares, with dots drawn on a results table and a bar chart with four bars.
setup.caption: 4. Count the ants on each square every 2 minutes and draw the totals as bars.

flow.do: Look for ants. Try the kitchen floor near the sink, the foot of a wall, a window sill or the pots on a balcony. Pick a place where ants are already walking in a line. Sit one arm's length away. Ask your child to guess which of the four foods the ants will visit most, and why. Write the guess on the table sheet.
flow.say: Four small foods are coming to the ant café. They are sugar water, salt water, plain water and a crumb of fried snack. Which will get the most ants? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find a line of ants. Sit an arm's length back. Guess which food gets the most ants, and say why.

ask.q: Which food will get the most ants, and why?
good: Sugar water, because ants like sweet things.
The oily crumb, because it is real food.
Any guess with a reason. The ants will give the answer.

flow.parent: A guess is never marked right or wrong. If you see no ants, put one drop of sugar water on a card near a kitchen corner, a window sill or a plant pot. Wait up to 15 minutes. If none come, try early morning, evening or another day. Nobody touches the ants.

flow.do: Make the foods. Stir 1 teaspoon of sugar into 2 tablespoons of water in one katori until it is clear. Do the same with 1 teaspoon of salt in a second katori. Pour 2 tablespoons of plain water into a third. Crush a pinch of fried snack into the fourth. Put the four tissue squares on the card in a row, 8 centimetres apart. Wet the first with half a teaspoon of sugar water. Wet the second with half a teaspoon of salt water. Wet the third with half a teaspoon of plain water. Put the crushed snack on the fourth. Write A, B, C and D under the squares and note which food is where.
flow.say: Each square is a small plate. We give every plate the same amount, so that only the food is different. Which square do you think the ants will find first?
flow.kid: Make the three liquids. Wet three tissue squares, one with each. Put crushed snack on the fourth. Put the squares in a row.
flow.parent: Use the same amount of liquid on each square. Very salty water may put ants off, and that is a result too. Keep the katoris covered afterwards so that they do not attract ants to the wrong place.

flow.do: Tape the card to the floor about 10 centimetres from the ant trail. Run the row of squares along the trail, so that each square is the same distance from the trail. Start the timer. At 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 minutes, count the ants standing on each square and write the numbers in the table. Note the minute when the first ant touches any square, and the minute when one square first holds 5 ants.
flow.say: Count only ants who are standing on a square, not ants walking past. Which square gets an ant first? Do more ants come after the first one?
flow.kid: Tape the card near the trail. Every 2 minutes, count the ants on each square. Write the numbers down.

ask.q: What happens on the winning square after the first ant arrives?
good: Many more ants come. The first ant leaves a smell trail and her sisters follow the trail.
It gets crowded fast, much faster than the first ant took to arrive.

flow.parent: Dot each ant on scrap paper as you count, so that your child can count again if the ants move. If no ant touches a square in 10 minutes, move the card up to 3 centimetres from the trail and start again. If still none, leave the card for an hour and count once then. Do not brush ants away, and do not block the trail.

flow.do: Reverse the row. The food at the left end goes to the right end, and the food at the right end goes to the left. The two in the middle swap places. Write which food is now on which square.
flow.say: Now every food is in a new place. Why would we move them?
flow.kid: Reverse the row of squares. Every food gets a new place.
flow.parent: This round checks whether ants just like the place nearest to where they arrive. If one food wins in both rounds, the food is the reason.

flow.do: Count again at 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 minutes, and write the numbers in the second part of the table.
flow.say: Is the same food winning? Or did the winner change when we moved the squares?
flow.kid: Count the ants on each square again, 5 times. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: The ants know the way by now, so more may arrive earlier in this round. That is the trail at work and a good thing to notice.

flow.do: Add each food's numbers from both rounds. Draw four bars, one for each food. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then wipe the card and the floor with a damp cloth, throw away the tissue squares and wash hands.
flow.say: Which food got the most ants in both rounds? Was your guess right? What do you think the ants were doing with the sugar?
flow.kid: Add up the ants for each food. Draw four bars. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.think: If a family found these same ants at the sugar in a tin, what would they call them? What did the ants do differently?
flow.parent: This test cannot tell us why the ants chose as they did, or whether the ants like the taste. It tells us about one ant family on one day. Ants of other kinds, or the same ants in another season, may choose differently. Some ants are hungry for fat or protein and ignore sugar. What else could your child test? A weaker or stronger sugar water, a different time of day, or a crumb of rice are good next questions.

experiments.title: The Wobble Test: why do walking insects never tip over?
experiments.question: A table on four legs can rock if the floor is a little uneven. A table on three legs never does. Is that true? What does it show about six-legged walkers?
experiments.predict: Guess which will rock when you tap it, a card on four caps or a card on three caps, when one cap is a little taller. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same card, the same caps, the same coins and the same table are used every time. Only the number of caps under the card changes, four or three. One cap is lifted by a small stack of coins, and each cap takes a turn at being the lifted one. Each setup is tapped 5 times in the middle with one finger.
results_table: Does the card rock? (yes or no)

materials.item: a stiff card about 10 centimetres square, cut from a cereal box
plastic bottle caps, all the same size
2 one-rupee coins
a flat table
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.record: Fill in the table for 4 caps and then for 3 caps. Write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why. Draw the card on three caps from the side, and mark where an insect's three steady legs would be.
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a small table from a card and bottle caps and test when it rocks. You find out why three legs always stand steadily, and why an insect who lifts three legs and keeps three down never tips.

setup.art: A square card resting on four bottle caps, one at each corner, on a flat table.
setup.caption: 1. Rest the card on four caps, one at each corner.

setup.art: A hand sliding two coins under one cap, so that one corner stands a little higher than the others.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one cap with two coins.

setup.art: A finger tapping the middle of the card, with the card rocking slightly on two caps.
setup.caption: 3. Tap the middle of the card 5 times. Listen for clicks.

setup.art: The same card resting on only three caps, one of them on coins, sitting still under a tapping finger.
setup.caption: 4. Take one cap away and tap again.

flow.do: Put the table on a flat, hard surface. Set the 4 caps upside down at the four corners of the card, under it, so that the card rests on them. Check that the card sits flat.
flow.say: This is a small table with four legs. When the floor is flat, it stands. What do you think will happen when one leg is slightly taller?
flow.kid: Rest the card on four caps, one at each corner.
flow.parent: Use caps that are all the same. Put the card on a flat, hard table, never a cloth or a bed.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess. Then lift one cap with two coins stacked under it and write the number of the lifted cap on the table.
flow.say: Tap the middle of the card with one finger. Will the card rock, or stay still? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess if the card will rock. Say why.

ask.q: Will the card on four caps rock when one cap is higher?
good: Yes, because the card can tip over the two caps that touch at opposite corners.
No, because the card is heavy. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.do: Tap the middle of the card 5 times with one finger. Count the clicks and note whether it rocks. Then lift each of the other three caps in turn and tap 5 times each. Write all four results.
flow.say: Is it the same every time? Which cap you lift does not seem to matter. Why might that be?
flow.kid: Tap the card 5 times. Count the clicks. Do it with each cap lifted in turn.
flow.parent: A rock sounds like a click-clack. A lifted cap leaves the card touching only two caps at opposite corners, and it tips back and forth over them.

flow.do: Take one cap away, so that the card rests on three caps placed in a triangle under it. Lift one cap with two coins. Tap 5 times and write the result. Do this with each of the three caps lifted in turn.
flow.say: Now there are only three legs. Which do you think will rock?
flow.kid: Use three caps. Lift one with coins. Tap 5 times. Does the card rock?
flow.parent: Place the three caps so that the card's middle sits inside the triangle they make. The card may tilt a little, and that is fine. Tilting is not rocking. A rock means the card tips back and forth.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Draw the card on three caps from the side.
flow.say: Which table never rocked? Why can three points always hold a flat card steady? An ant lifts three legs and keeps three down. What shape do her feet make on the ground?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why. Draw the card on three caps from the side.
flow.think: Could a walker with four legs lift two at a time and stay steady? What would you test?
flow.parent: Three points always make a flat triangle, and a card can rest on a triangle without rocking. This test cannot show how a real insect walks. Real feet have sticky pads and claws, and real insects also run so fast that they glide. Engineers who copy the tripod walk in six-legged robots have to test them on real rubble.

activities.title: Be an antenna: find the matching smells with your eyes shut
activities.context: In this activity you use your nose the way an insect uses her antennae. You match pairs of smells without looking, and then find how far away you can still smell one.

materials.item: 6 small cups or katoris
6 pieces of thin cloth or kitchen tissue, with rubber bands, to cover the cups
2 cloves, a pinch of tea leaves and a small piece of orange or lemon peel, each in two lots
a scarf or a cloth to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes

schedule.what: Make six smell cups, match the pairs, then test how far away you can smell a clove.

activities.record: Draw the six cups and join the matching pairs with lines. Write the distance in steps at which you could first smell the clove.

setup.art: Six small cups in a row, each covered with a cloth held by a rubber band, with a clove, tea leaves and orange peel beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put each smell in two cups and cover every cup with cloth.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut holding one covered cup near the nose, with a parent shuffling the other cups.
setup.caption: 2. With eyes shut, sniff the cups and find the matching pairs.

setup.art: A child standing at one end of a hall while a parent walks back with a cup of crushed clove, holding a hand up.
setup.caption: 3. Find how far away you can still smell the clove.

flow.do: Put two cloves, crushed, into two cups. Put a pinch of tea leaves into two more cups. Put a piece of squeezed orange or lemon peel into the last two. Cover each cup with cloth and a rubber band. Shuffle the cups so that you do not know which are pairs.
flow.say: An insect has no nose on her face. She smells with her antennae. Today you will smell with your nose, and match pairs the way an ant checks that another ant smells like her nest.
flow.kid: Make six covered cups, two of each smell. Shuffle them.
flow.parent: Do the shuffling out of your child's sight, so that the pairs are a surprise. If you have no orange or lemon peel, use a pinch of turmeric or a small piece of jaggery.

flow.do: Ask your child to close their eyes or wear the scarf. Hand over one cup at a time. They sniff it and put it into a pile. They find the three pairs by smell alone. Then they open their eyes and check.
flow.say: Take a good sniff. Which two cups smell the same? Do not peek. How did you decide?
flow.kid: Sniff each cup with your eyes shut. Put matching cups together. Then open your eyes and check.

ask.q: How did you tell the smells apart?
good: By how strong they were, and by whether they were sweet or sharp.
I remembered the first smell and compared the next one with it.

flow.parent: If your child struggles, give a break after 3 or 4 sniffs. The nose gets tired and then smells everything the same. A breath of fresh air resets it.

flow.do: Crush a fresh clove and hold it in your open palm. Ask your child to stand at one end of a room with eyes shut. Walk slowly towards them from the far end of a room until they say they can smell it. Count the steps between you.
flow.say: A male silk moth can smell a female silk moth from very far away. How far can you smell the clove?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Say 'now' when you smell the clove. Count the steps between you.
flow.think: If you could smell as well as a moth, how would your day change?
flow.parent: A room with a fan or open windows moves the smell around, so your child may smell it from the side before you reach them. That is a good thing to talk about. Moths use the wind too.

activities.title: A fly's-eye picture: draw it in a few big squares and in many small ones
activities.context: In this activity you draw the same picture twice, once with big squares and once with small squares. You see how an eye made of many small units makes a picture, and why more units give a clearer one.

materials.item: a squared notebook page or paper with a grid drawn by hand
coloured pencils: red, yellow, green and blue
a ruler
a simple picture to copy, such as a red flower with a yellow centre on a green stem

schedule.what: Draw a simple picture on a grid of 16 big squares, then on a grid of 64 small squares, and compare.

activities.record: Keep both pictures. Write one sentence on which picture shows the flower better, and one on which one a moving object would be easier to notice in.

setup.art: A square grid of 4 by 4 big squares, each filled with one colour, forming a rough picture of a red flower.
setup.caption: 1. Fill each of 16 big squares with one colour.

setup.art: The same picture drawn on a grid of 8 by 8 small squares, clearer than the first, with petals and a stem.
setup.caption: 2. Fill 64 small squares with one colour each.

setup.art: The two pictures side by side, with a bee and a dragonfly drawn above them.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the pictures. More lenses show more detail.

flow.do: Look at the picture to copy. Draw a square 12 centimetres wide on paper. Divide it into 16 equal squares, 4 across and 4 down.
flow.say: A compound eye is made of many tiny lenses, and each lens sees one small patch. Your brain joins the patches. We will make a picture the same way.
flow.kid: Draw a big square. Divide it into 16 equal squares.
flow.parent: On squared paper, a block of 3 small squares by 3 small squares counts as one big square. A 12 centimetre square split into 4 by 4 gives squares of 3 centimetres.

flow.do: Fill each of the 16 squares with one colour only. Use the colour that fills most of that square in the real picture. Do not draw lines inside a square.
flow.say: Each square is one lens of an eye. It can show only one colour. Can you still see a flower?
flow.kid: Fill each square with one colour only. Make a flower picture.

ask.q: Can you tell it is a flower?
good: Yes, a rough one. I can see red in the middle and green below.
Barely. The squares are too big to show a petal.

flow.do: Draw a second square of the same size, divided into 64 equal squares, 8 across and 8 down. Fill each with one colour. This will take a while, so take turns with a grown-up if your child likes.
flow.say: Now each lens is much smaller. There are four times as many lenses. What can you see now that you could not before?
flow.kid: Draw the second square with 64 small squares. Fill each with one colour.
flow.parent: This is a rough model. A real compound eye has thousands of lenses, so the world is made of tiny patches too. A fly or a dragonfly sees movement very well because a moving thing passes from one unit to the next.

flow.do: Put the two pictures side by side. Ask your child which shows the flower better. Then ask how a moving bee would look in each: crossing one big square, or 4 small ones.
flow.say: Which picture shows more detail? Which has more lenses? Why might many lenses help to catch something moving?
flow.kid: Compare the pictures. Which shows more? Why?
flow.think: A bee has about 5,000 lenses in each eye and a dragonfly up to about 30,000. What does a dragonfly see that a bee does not?
flow.parent: A bee sees ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see, and is poor at seeing red. Compound eyes make a less sharp picture than ours but catch movement very well. We cannot know exactly what an insect sees, only what the eye can and cannot sense.

activities.title: Wear an outside skeleton: why an insect must moult
activities.context: In this activity you make a stiff card tube for your forearm, as a model of an insect's outside skeleton. You find out why a hard cover needs joints, and why an insect must change her cover as she grows.

materials.item: a flattened empty cereal box
blunt scissors
sticky tape
a thin strip of cloth, about 10 centimetres by 2 centimetres, or more tape

schedule.what: Make a card tube for the forearm, try to bend the elbow, add joints, then see what happens when the arm grows.

activities.record: Draw your arm in its card tube with the joints marked. Write one sentence about what happens to a hard tube when the arm inside it grows.

setup.art: A child holding a rolled stiff card tube around the forearm, elbow straight, unable to bend.
setup.caption: 1. Roll a stiff card tube around the forearm and tape it.

setup.art: A card tube cut into three rings joined by thin strips of tape across the back, bending at the elbow.
setup.caption: 2. Cut the tube into rings and join them with soft strips.

setup.art: A child's arm too thick for the old tube, with a bigger new tube lying beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Make a bigger tube. This is what a moult does.

flow.do: Roll a stiff card around your child's forearm, from the wrist to the elbow, loosely enough to slide off. Tape the edge so the card stays a tube. Slide it back on. Ask your child to bend the elbow.
flow.say: An insect wears her skeleton on the outside, like a suit of armour. This tube is armour for your arm. Can you bend your elbow?
flow.kid: Put the tube on your forearm. Try to bend your elbow.

ask.q: What happens when you try to bend your arm?
good: The tube is in the way. It does not bend.
I can only bend where there is no tube.

flow.parent: Keep the tube loose so your child can slide the arm in and out. A tube that is tight can pinch.

flow.do: Take the tube off. Draw two lines around it, dividing it into three equal rings. Cut along the lines, with the adult doing the cutting, to make three rings. Tape the three rings together on one side. Use strips of tape or cloth, and leave a gap of about 1 centimetre between rings. Slide the tube back on and bend the elbow.
flow.say: Insect legs have hard tubes with soft joints in between. Now where can your arm bend?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the tube into three rings. Join the rings with soft strips. Bend your elbow.
flow.parent: Cutting card with scissors is an adult job in this step. The child can hold the card and draw the lines. A gap of 1 centimetre between rings is what lets the arm bend. This is how an insect leg works: hard sections joined by soft skin.

flow.do: Now pretend your child's arm grows. Wrap a thick folded cloth or a rolled sock around the forearm, to make it thicker. Try to put the card tube back on over it. Then make a bigger tube from a new piece of card, with a wider roll.
flow.say: The arm grew. The old tube is too small. What does a growing insect have to do?
flow.kid: Wrap a sock around your arm. Try the old tube. Make a bigger tube.

ask.q: What does a growing insect need to do with her old skin?
good: Get out of it and make a new, bigger one. That is moulting.
She has to split it, climb out and grow a bigger one.

flow.parent: The insect makes a new soft skin under the old one, splits the old skin, climbs out and swells with air. The new skin is soft and easy to hurt for a few hours until it hardens. A card tube cannot stretch, and nor can a hard exoskeleton.

flow.do: Look at both tubes. Draw your arm in the joined tube with the joints marked. Write one sentence about what happens to a hard tube when the arm inside it grows.
flow.say: What is the good thing about a hard outside skeleton? What is the problem with it?
flow.kid: Draw your arm in the joined tube. Write what a growing arm needs.
flow.think: While a newly moulted insect is soft, what could happen to her? How could she stay safe?
flow.parent: Hard armour protects and stops the insect drying out. The price is that she must moult, and she is soft and easy to hurt until the new skin hardens. Many insects moult in hiding, at night or under leaves.

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors. Keep the card tube loose on the arm.

activities.title: Walk the thread: how far is one silk cocoon's thread?
activities.context: In this activity you measure your own steps and use them to find how long a walk equals the thread of one silk cocoon. You find how far one silkworm's thread reaches.

materials.item: a measuring tape or a long string with a 10 metre mark
a clear walking path of 10 metres, such as a corridor, a terrace or a lane
a phone with a stopwatch
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Walk 10 metres, count steps and time yourself, then work out how many steps and minutes a cocoon's thread would take.

activities.record: Write the steps and the seconds for 10 metres. Write how many steps and how many minutes it would take to walk 800 metres, and 1 kilometre.

setup.art: A child walking along a corridor beside a tape laid on the floor with a mark at 10 metres.
setup.caption: 1. Measure 10 metres on the floor.

setup.art: A parent timing a child with a phone while the child counts steps aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Walk it at your ordinary pace. Count steps and time.

setup.art: A drawing of a cocoon beside a long line of footprints going off the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Work out how long a walk the thread of one cocoon is.

flow.do: Measure 10 metres along a floor or path, and mark the start and the end. A strip of paper tape at each end will do.
flow.say: A silkworm spins one long thread to make her cocoon. It can be several hundred metres, and sometimes about a kilometre. We will find out how long a walk that is.
flow.kid: Measure 10 metres. Mark the start and the end.
flow.parent: No tape measure? Use a string marked every 1 metre against a metre ruler or a tailor's tape. Or count 10 long strides of an adult and call that about 10 metres.

flow.do: Ask your child to walk the 10 metres at an ordinary pace and count the steps. Time the walk with the phone. Do it 3 times and use the middle value of the three.
flow.say: Walk like you are going to school. Count each step. Do we get the same number each time?
flow.kid: Walk 10 metres. Count your steps. Time it. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Three tries are done because one try can be a fluke. Choose the middle value of the three. If your child's steps are different each time, that is real, and it is why we take the middle.

flow.do: Work out together. Divide 800 metres by 10 to find how many lots of 10 metres, then multiply by the steps for 10 metres. Do the same for the seconds. Then do the same for 1 kilometre.
flow.say: How many steps would it take to walk the thread of one cocoon, if it is 800 metres long? How many minutes?
flow.kid: Work out the steps and the minutes for 800 metres. Then for 1 kilometre.

ask.q: About how long would you walk to follow one cocoon's thread?
good: Around 10 minutes or more, depending on how fast I walk.
A lot more steps than I thought, around a thousand.

flow.parent: Example: 14 steps for 10 metres and 9 seconds. For 800 metres, 80 lots of 10 gives 1,120 steps and 720 seconds, which is 12 minutes. A cocoon's thread is often several hundred metres, and can reach about a kilometre.

flow.do: Say the answer in a sentence. Ask where in your lane or school the walk would end.
flow.say: Where would you be after one cocoon's walk? Who made this thread? How long might she have taken?
flow.kid: Write one sentence with your answer. Say where the walk would end.
flow.think: A silkworm makes all of that thread inside her own body. What do you think that is like?
flow.parent: A silkworm makes the thread inside her body and pushes the thread out near her mouth. She takes a few days to spin the cocoon. The thread is one unbroken line, which is why it can be unwound and woven.

activities.title: Still-water hunt: find where water stands still in your home
activities.context: In this activity you walk around your home and make a map of every place where water stands still for days. You find where mosquito young could grow, and tip the water out.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a torch
a clipboard or a book to lean on

schedule.what: Draw a rough plan of the home, find still water, and tip it out. Do it again every week.

activities.record: A rough plan of your home and balcony with a cross at every place where water stood. A list of what you found and what you did.

setup.art: A child drawing a rough plan of a flat with a balcony on a clipboard, a parent beside.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a rough plan of your home and balcony.

setup.art: A child shining a torch into a flowerpot tray with a little water in it.
setup.caption: 2. Look for water that stands still, with a torch in dark corners.

setup.art: A child tipping a tray of water onto dry ground, with a cross on the plan.
setup.caption: 3. Tip each one out and mark it on the plan.

flow.do: Draw a rough plan of your home, with the balcony or terrace and the front step. Do not draw it carefully. Boxes and labels are enough.
flow.say: Some mosquitoes lay their eggs on still water. Their young live in it for about a week or more. Where in our home does water stay still for days?
flow.kid: Draw a rough plan of your home. Add the balcony or terrace.
flow.parent: Mosquitoes that carry dengue like small pools of clean water. Others prefer dirty water. Both need water that is not moving.

flow.do: Walk through every room and outside. Look in flowerpot trays, buckets, a cooler's tank and a fridge tray. Then look in old tins, coconut shells, plant saucers, tyres and folds of plastic sheet. Use the torch in dark corners. Write each place on the plan, and put a cross where there is still water.
flow.say: Look for any water that has stood for more than 2 days. Use the torch to look into dark places. Where might small wrigglers be?
flow.kid: Find every place where water stands. Put a cross on your plan.

ask.q: Which place had the most water standing?
good: A flowerpot tray, or the cooler.
Any real place from the home. A bucket, a tin or a tray are all common.

flow.parent: If you find tiny comma-shaped wrigglers hanging at the surface, watch them for one minute first. They dive when a shadow falls over them. Then tip out the water onto dry ground away from the home. This is a choice to protect people from illness, and it is worth talking about. Check roof tanks only with a grown-up, and never climb a ladder alone.

flow.do: Tip out each place that has still water, onto dry ground. Scrub the pot or tray with a brush to remove eggs. Turn buckets upside down. Cover water you must keep, such as a drinking-water pot, with a tight lid or a cloth.
flow.say: Empty and scrub. Why do you think we scrub, not just tip?
flow.kid: Tip out the water. Scrub the pot. Turn buckets over.
flow.parent: Mosquito eggs stick to the sides of a container just above the water line and can wait there for months. Scrubbing removes them. A grown-up should handle heavy buckets and any tank or roof item.

flow.do: Put a weekly reminder on the fridge to do the hunt again. Ask your child which place will fill up again fastest after a rain.
flow.say: Which of your crosses will fill again first? Why do we need to do this every week?
flow.kid: Put a note on the fridge: do the still-water hunt every week.
flow.think: The mosquito young are eaten by fish and dragonfly nymphs. Why might emptying the water still matter?
flow.parent: Young mosquitoes take about a week or a little more to become adults in warm weather. Emptying once a week breaks the cycle. Where water cannot be emptied, guppies or gambusia fish eat the young, and local health offices give these fish free in many places.

activities.safety: Check roof tanks and high places only with a grown-up. Wash your hands after handling pots and trays.

projects.title: Friend or foe? What is each insect doing: a six-day plant watch
projects.context: In this project you watch one plant for ten minutes a day, for five days, and write down every insect and what she is doing. On the sixth day you see that one insect can do harmful and helpful things.

materials.item: one plant with leaves or flowers, a pot on a balcony, a tree, or a weed on a footpath
a notebook and a pencil
a clock or phone for 10 minutes
a magnifying glass, optional

schedule.what: Choose a plant, then draw the plant and make your first watch.
Watch for insects who eat the leaves or stems.
Watch for insects who visit the flowers or sit on the fruit.
Watch under the leaves and on the stem, for insects who hunt others.
Watch in the evening, for who comes at a different time.
Sort the week's records, and decide what each insect is called.

projects.record: A table with five columns: day, who (drawing or words), six legs or not, what she is doing, and what that does for the plant. On day 6, a second sheet with one line for each different insect: the doings, and what she would be called in each.

setup.art: A child sitting a metre from a curry-leaf plant in a pot on a balcony, with a notebook open on the knee.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one plant. Sit a metre away and watch for ten minutes.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of columns for day, who, doing and effect, with small drawings of an ant and a fly.
setup.caption: 2. Write or draw each insect and what she is doing.

setup.art: A notebook page with lines linking one insect to two different doings with two different labels.
setup.caption: 3. On day 6, link each insect to every doing you saw.

flow.do: Choose a plant. A pot on a balcony, a tree outside the building, or a weed with flowers on a footpath will do. Draw the whole plant. Sit one metre away and watch it for 10 minutes. Write or draw every insect you see and what she is doing.
flow.say: Insects are everywhere, even on one small plant. Today, do not name anyone friend or foe. Just write what each one is doing.
flow.kid: Pick a plant. Draw it. Watch for 10 minutes. Write what each insect is doing.
flow.parent: Keep a metre away and never touch. If bees or wasps are around, keep a bigger gap and stay calm and still. Do not disturb a nest. If you see no insects, write 'none seen' and watch another plant tomorrow. That is a result too. A plant in flower will draw more visitors.

ask.q: What is the insect doing on the plant?
good: Eating a leaf, drinking from a flower, walking along the stem, or resting.
Any honest answer. 'I do not know' is fine, and so is a drawing.

flow.do: At the same time of day, watch for 10 minutes. Look for insects who are eating the plant: holes in a leaf, a caterpillar, small insects clustered on a stem. Write who and what she is doing. Check if the legs are six, using the magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: Look for who is eating the plant today. What do the leaves look like where she is eating?
flow.kid: Same time as yesterday. Look for who is eating the plant.
flow.parent: Do the watch at the same time each day, so that the comparison is fair. Check six legs if you can see them. A spider is not an insect and goes in the notes as 'a spider, eight legs'.

flow.do: Watch for insects who visit the flower or sit on the fruit. Write who, and what she is doing. Does she touch the middle of the flower? Does she carry anything on her legs or body?
flow.say: Look at the flowers. Who comes? What does she do when she lands?
flow.kid: Same time again. Watch the flowers. Write who comes and what she does.
flow.parent: No flowers? Watch a different plant for this day only, such as a weed with tiny flowers on a path. Flies are as good a visitor as bees.

flow.do: Watch under the leaves and along the stem. Look for insects who hunt others, or who carry something, such as ants carrying a dead insect. Write who and what she is doing. Look under three leaves, gently, with your eyes only.
flow.say: Look under three leaves. Is anybody hunting? Is anybody being hunted?
flow.kid: Look under three leaves with your eyes. Write who is there and what she is doing.
flow.parent: Do not turn leaves with fingers if you are not sure what is under them. Look from the side, or lean a little to see underneath.

flow.do: Watch in the evening, at dusk, instead of the usual time. Write who is there that you did not see earlier, and who is missing.
flow.say: Is the plant the same at dusk? Is anybody new? Is anybody gone?
flow.kid: Watch at dusk. Write who is new and who is gone.
flow.parent: Evening watchers include moths and mosquitoes, so keep your distance and wash hands after. Stay where a grown-up can see you, and do not go out in the dark alone.

flow.do: Read through the week's notes together. Put each different insect on a line. Next to her, write every doing you saw. Then, for each doing, ask the question: would the plant's owner call this helpful, harmful or neither? Look for any insect who has two different labels.
flow.say: Did any insect do two different things? What would the plant's owner call her in each? What do you think the plant would say?
flow.kid: Sort your notes by insect. Write all her doings. Give each doing a label: helpful, harmful or neither.
flow.think: Is 'friend' or 'foe' a part of the insect, or a result of where she is and what we want? How would you decide?
flow.parent: Many records will show only one doing for each insect. That is fine, and the question is still open for your child to answer. A caterpillar who eats the leaf becomes a butterfly who visits flowers. An ant in the sugar tin is the same as an ant on a plant stem. The label belongs to where she is and what we want.

projects.safety: Stay a metre from the plant. Never touch an insect, and keep well away from bees, wasps and any nest. Wash your hands with soap afterwards.

challenges.title: Ant-proof the sugar: keep ants away with no poison and no harm
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Ants find sugar in a kitchen. You design and test a way to keep them out of a sugar bowl that does not poison or hurt them.
challenges.problem: Keep ants out of a small bowl of sugar for 30 minutes, with no poison and no harm to the ants. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: No sprays or poison of any kind, and nothing that hurts or traps ants. A chalk line or a ring of ground cinnamon is allowed.
The sugar must stay open enough that you could scoop it out with a spoon.
Test each design for 10 minutes beside a real ant trail, and count how many ants reach the sugar.
If an ant falls into water, lift her out with a leaf or a strip of paper.
materials: a small bowl of sugar, about 2 tablespoons, for each design
a large plate, a tin lid or a tray
water, shallow and no deeper than 5 millimetres
a lid, a plate or a cloth cover
chalk, a pinch of cinnamon or cloves
string and a hook, for hanging

setup.art: A bowl of sugar on a plate on the floor near an ant trail, with ants walking toward the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Put an open bowl of sugar near a trail and watch how ants reach the sugar.

setup.art: A bowl of sugar standing in the middle of a plate filled with shallow water.
setup.caption: 2. Try the usual fixes: a lid, or a plate with a shallow moat.

setup.art: A bowl of sugar hanging from a string above the floor, with a second feeding spot of sugar crumbs on a balcony.
setup.caption: 3. Try a creative idea, such as a hanging bowl or a separate feeding spot.

flow.do: Put a small bowl of open sugar beside an ant trail on a plate. Watch for 3 minutes. Note how the ants reach the sugar, and which way they come. Draw the route.
flow.say: How do the ants get to the sugar? Look closely. Which way do they come in?
flow.kid: Watch how the ants reach the sugar. Draw their route.
flow.parent: Ants follow a smell trail that the first ant leaves. If the first test brings no ants in 10 minutes, move the plate closer to the trail or leave a few grains for a few minutes. Wash hands after, and do not touch ants.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes one by one, for 5 minutes each. A tight lid. The bowl standing on a plate with a shallow ring of water around it. A cloth wiped along the trail with damp water, to remove the smell. Count how many ants reach the sugar for each.
flow.say: Which of these gives the fewest ants? Why might the water ring work?
flow.kid: Try a lid. Try a bowl in a water ring. Wipe the trail. Count the ants for each.

ask.q: Which fix kept the most ants away?
good: The lid, because ants cannot get in.
The water ring, because ants cannot cross it and the rest turn back.

flow.parent: Keep the water ring shallow, about 5 millimetres. Lift any ant who falls in with a paper strip. If ants build a bridge from a crumb, that is clever and worth noticing.

flow.do: Try a creative fix. Hang the bowl from a string so that nothing touches it. Or draw a thick chalk line or sprinkle cinnamon in a ring. Or put a few sugar crumbs on a saucer on the balcony as a separate feeding spot for the ants. Count again.
flow.say: What else could keep ants away? Could you give them somewhere else to go?
flow.kid: Try a hanging bowl, a chalk or cinnamon ring, or a different feeding spot.
flow.parent: No result is wrong. Chalk and cinnamon work for some ants and not for others. A separate feeding spot teaches that we can share, but it is not a solution for every home. Say so honestly.

flow.do: Design your own. Draw your plan, build it and test it for 10 minutes. Count the ants. Write which designs worked best and what each costs in time, tidiness or the ants' good.
flow.say: What is your own idea? How will you know it worked? What does it cost?
flow.kid: Draw your own plan. Build it. Test it for 10 minutes. Count the ants.
flow.think: Is keeping ants out the same as keeping them away from their food? Whose food is the sugar?
flow.parent: A good answer has a plan, a count and an honest note on what it costs. Wipe up all the sugar at the end, wash the plate and your hands.

general: A tight lid on a sugar tin, so that ants cannot get in.
A bowl standing in a plate of shallow water, like a moat.
Wiping the ant trail with a damp cloth, so that the first ant's smell is gone.
Sealing the crack where the ants come in.
creative: Hang the sugar bowl from a string so that no surface touches it.
Draw a thick chalk line or a ring of cinnamon around the bowl, and see whether ants cross.
Give the ants their own feeding spot far away, with a few crumbs, so they stop looking for the tin.
Put the bowl on a stand with four legs, each in a small cup of water.
challenges.your_turn: Design a way that keeps ants away from the sugar and is kind to them. Draw it, build it, test it for 10 minutes, and tell which parts worked. There is more than one good answer, and none of the answers is ranked as best.
challenges.safety: Some ants bite, so never use your fingers to move one. Use a leaf or a strip of paper. When you finish, clean up the sugar and the plate so that no trail leads into the kitchen.

challenges.title: A lid for the water pot: keep mosquitoes out and still let the family dip a mug
challenges.context: This is a design problem. A family keeps drinking water in an open pot, and mosquitoes could lay eggs in it. You design a cover that keeps small insects out but is easy to use.
challenges.problem: Design a cover for a pot of water that stops mustard seeds from falling in. The seeds stand in for a mosquito. The cover must still let someone dip a mug quickly. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: The family must be able to dip a mug without taking the whole cover off.
The cover must stay on without a person holding it.
Test with 20 mustard seeds sprinkled on the cover and a gentle shake, and count how many reach the water.
Use only things you can find at home.
materials: a wide pot, bucket or large bowl
a net curtain scrap, a muslin cloth or an old dupatta
a plate that fits the top of the pot
scissors, for an adult to use

setup.art: A pot of water with a cloth stretched over it and tied tight with a rubber band, with mustard seeds scattered on top.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a cloth over the pot and tie it. Sprinkle 20 mustard seeds on it.

setup.art: A hand tilting a cloth cover to see how many mustard seeds slid into the water, with a count beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Shake the pot a little. Count the seeds that fell through.

setup.art: A cloth cover with a small slit and a flap of cloth over it, with a mug being dipped through the slit.
setup.caption: 3. Try a design with a flap, so that a mug can go in.

flow.do: Stretch a cloth over the pot of water. Tie it with a rubber band or string. Sprinkle 20 mustard seeds on the cloth. Shake it gently for a count of 10. Count how many fell into the water.
flow.say: A mosquito is small. The mustard seed is about as thick as a small mosquito's body. If the seed goes through, a mosquito might too. How many fell in?
flow.kid: Tie a cloth over the pot. Sprinkle 20 seeds. Shake gently. Count how many fell in.
flow.parent: A mustard seed is a rough stand-in for a mosquito, and not a perfect one. Real mosquito nets use holes finer than a mustard seed. Do not put any real mosquitoes or wrigglers into this test.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes, 5 minutes each. A tight cloth with a rubber band. A plate on top. A double-layered cloth. Test each with 20 mustard seeds. Then see if you can dip a mug.
flow.say: Which one holds back the most seeds? Which is easy to use for dipping?
flow.kid: Try a cloth, a plate and a double cloth. Count the seeds each time. Try dipping a mug.

ask.q: Which cover stopped the most seeds, and which was easiest to use?
good: A plate stops them all, but is hard to dip through. A thin cloth lets some through.
The double cloth did well. Any honest answer from the test.

flow.parent: A plate stops all seeds, but dipping means lifting it, which opens a gap. A thin cloth lets seeds through. A tight, fine cloth is good but sags. The problem is to find a way to do both jobs.

flow.do: Try a creative idea. Make a cloth cover with a slit and a loose flap that closes on its own. Or add a ring of cloth that stands up around a hole. Or make a sleeve of cloth for the mug. Test with 20 seeds again. Then dip a mug.
flow.say: Can you make a door? Can you make something that closes by itself?
flow.kid: Make a cover with a flap or a slit. Test it with 20 seeds. Dip a mug.
flow.parent: An adult cuts the slit. A flap that overlaps by 3 centimetres will fall shut by its own weight. Fine mesh with no gaps at the edge is the key. Seeds can slip under the rim, so tie the cloth snugly.

flow.do: Draw your own design. Build it and test it with 20 seeds. Write which design was best, and what a family would need to do each week to keep the water safe.
flow.say: What is your design? How many seeds got in? What would your family have to do every week?
flow.kid: Draw your own cover. Test it. Write the count.
flow.think: Even a perfect cover does not help if the pot is left uncovered for a night. How could a family remember?
flow.parent: A cover helps, and so does emptying and scrubbing the pot every week. Neither alone is complete. A real family chooses what suits their home. There is no one right design.

general: A tight, fine cloth tied over the top of the pot with a rubber band.
A plate or lid that fits the pot, lifted only to dip.
A double layer of cloth, so that gaps do not line up.
A tap fitted near the bottom of the pot, so no dipping is needed.
creative: A cloth cover with a slit and a flap that closes by its own weight.
A cloth funnel that lets a mug in and out but sags shut.
A pot with a small spout, so that water can be poured out without opening the top.
A pot kept in a net bag, tied at the neck.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own cover for a water pot. Draw it, build it from things at home, test it with 20 mustard seeds and a mug, and tell what worked. There is more than one good answer.
challenges.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors. Wash your hands after handling the pot. The test water gets mustard seeds in it, so do not drink it.

worksheets.title: Insect or not, growing up and helping (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can tell an insect from other small animals and name her body parts. It also checks that you can follow how she grows and say what the word 'pest' means.

items.p: A beetle, a spider and a bee sit on one leaf. How many legs are there altogether?
items.why: A beetle has 6 legs, a spider has 8 and a bee has 6. 6 + 8 + 6 = 20. If you got 18, you gave the spider six legs.

items.p: Label a worker bee: head, thorax, abdomen, antenna and one wing.
a: head: the front part, with the eyes and the mouth
thorax: the middle part, where the legs and wings join
antenna: a feeler on the head
items.why: An insect's body has three parts. The legs and wings join the middle part, and the feelers are on the head.
items.art: A honeybee seen from the side, with five empty label lines pointing to the head, the middle, the back, a feeler and a wing.

items.p: Sort each small animal. Is she an insect or not?
items.a: as given
items.why: An insect has six legs and three body parts. A spider has eight legs, a centipede has many and a woodlouse has fourteen.

items.p: An insect wears her skeleton on the outside of her body.
items.why: True. Her skeleton is a hard cover on the outside, called an exoskeleton. Yours is inside you.

items.p: Shedding an old hard skin so that a bigger one can harden is called ________.
items.why: A growing insect cannot stretch her hard cover, so she sheds it. This is moulting.

items.p: Match each young insect to the adult she becomes.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each young one lives a different life from her adult. The silkworm eats leaves and the moth does not eat at all.

items.p: Put the stages of a silk moth in order.
items.why: The egg hatches into a silkworm. She spins a cocoon, becomes a pupa, and a moth comes out.

items.p: Which of these crops usually gives more when insects visit the flowers?
opts: Mustard
Wheat
Maize
items.why: Mustard flowers are visited by bees and other insects, who carry pollen. Wheat and maize do not need insects to carry their pollen.

items.p: Every kind of bee lives in a hive.
items.why: False. A carpenter bee nests alone in a hole in wood. Most kinds of bees do not live in hives.

items.p: Match each insect to her work.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each insect has her own way of living, and people benefit from some of them. A farmer who protects hunters needs less spray.

items.p: Ants in the sugar tin are called pests. The same ants carrying a dead moth away are called helpers. What changed?
items.a: The ants did not change. What changed is the place and what they were doing. In the tin they take our sugar, and on the balcony they clear away a dead moth.
items.why: A strong answer says that the name depends on the place and on what we want, and the insect is the same one. 'Pest' is a name for a meeting between ants and our plans.

items.p: Draw the three stages of a grasshopper: egg, nymph and adult. Show how the wings change.
items.a: An egg, then a nymph that looks like a small grasshopper with tiny wing buds, then an adult with long working wings.
items.why: A grasshopper has no pupa. The nymph looks like a small adult, and her wings grow with each moult.

items.p: A line of ants has found the sugar tin in a flat.

views.says: Shut the tin tightly and wipe the shelf. The ants will go away by themselves.
Leave a few crumbs on the balcony for them. They will stop coming to the tin.
Use an ant-killing spray. It is quick, and the tin is safe in a day.

items.ask: Which would you choose at home? Say why, and say one thing another view gets right.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one and gives a reason. The lid and the crumb ways keep the ants alive and leave no poison near food. The spray is quick, and it also leaves poison in a kitchen and kills ants who were only looking for food.
items.why: A sealed tin solves the problem without harm. The crumb idea gives the ants somewhere else to go. A spray works fast but harms the ants and leaves a poison where food is kept.

items.p: Three of these are insects. Which is the odd one out? Ladybird, mosquito, scorpion, termite.
items.a: Scorpion. She has eight legs and two body parts, like a spider.
items.why: A scorpion is an arthropod, like insects, but not an insect.

items.p: Scientists still disagree about whether insects feel.
items.why: True. Some scientists point to play, mood and learning as signs of feeling. Others say these are automatic responses. The question is still open.

worksheets.title: Why insects are built and grow this way (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to explain how insects walk, see and grow, and to weigh what scientists still argue about.

items.p: A fly escapes before your hand lands. Which part of her body helps most?
opts: Her abdomen, which is large
Her compound eyes, which catch movement fast
Her sticky feet
items.why: A compound eye is made of many tiny lenses, each looking in a slightly different direction. The picture is less sharp than ours and very good at catching movement.

items.p: A walking insect keeps three legs on the ground while the other three move.
items.why: True. The three on the ground always make a steady triangle. Then the two sets of legs swap.

items.p: A caterpillar has a row of small dots along her side. What are they?
opts: Breathing holes called spiracles
Eyes
Ears
items.why: Spiracles open into thin air tubes that carry air to every part of her body. An insect has no lungs.

items.p: A bee sees a red flower as bright red, just as you do.
items.why: False. Bees do not see red well. They do see ultraviolet, which we cannot see.

items.p: Sort each insect by how she grows up.
items.a: as given
items.why: An insect with a nymph has three stages, and an insect with a larva and a pupa has four.

items.p: Empty skins hang on the reeds beside a pond. Where did they come from?
opts: Dead dragonflies
Dragonfly nymphs who moulted once more and flew off
Snakes who shed their skins
items.why: A dragonfly nymph climbs a reed, moults one last time and flies away as an adult. The empty skin stays on the reed.

items.p: The banyan, like other wild fig trees, can make its seeds without any wasp at all.
items.why: False. The banyan's flowers are hidden inside the fig, and only its own kind of tiny wasp can carry pollen in. Each one needs the other.

items.p: A farmer finds aphids on her chilli plants and a ladybird nearby. What is a bee-safe first step?
opts: Spray every leaf at noon
Cut the plant down
Wait a few days and watch the ladybird
items.why: A ladybird and her young eat dozens of aphids a day. Waiting gives the hunter time to work, and a spray would harm her and any bees.

items.p: Young mosquitoes live in still water. Explain why tipping out the water every week stops them.
items.a: They need about 8 days or more in water to become adults. If the water is gone before that, they cannot finish growing.
items.why: A good answer says that the young need still water for more than a week, so emptying it sooner breaks their life.

items.p: A lone desert locust harms nobody. In a crowd she joins a swarm. What does this say about calling locusts 'pests'?
items.a: It is the crowd and the place, not the kind of insect, that makes the trouble. The same animal is quiet alone and a swarm in a crowd.
items.why: A strong answer says that 'pest' describes the situation with people. The locust is the same animal.

items.p: Only a small share of insect kinds ever damage crops or carry illness.
items.why: True. A few thousand kinds do harm, out of about ten lakh named. That is well under one in a hundred.

items.p: A locust swarm covers 2 square kilometres. Each square kilometre eats the daily food of 35,000 people. How many people's food?
items.why: 35,000 × 2 = 70,000. The same swarm eating for 3 days would eat 2,10,000 people's food.

items.p: Draw one plain yellow flower twice: once as you see the flower, and once as a bee sees the same flower.
items.a: The first flower is plain yellow. The second has dark lines pointing to the middle, which a bee sees in ultraviolet light.
items.why: Many flowers have ultraviolet marks that point to the nectar. We cannot see them, and a bee can.

items.p: Do insects feel? Two scientists read the same evidence in different ways.

views.who: Lars Chittka, who studies bee minds
views.says: In his reading, bees learn, count and play, and a worried bee treats an uncertain smell as bad. This is hard to explain without feeling.

views.who: Shelley Adamo, who studies insect nerves
views.says: In her reading, these could be automatic responses with nobody feeling them. The evidence is not enough to say.

items.ask: Whose reading do you find stronger, and what would you test? Give a reason.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one reading and gives a reason. Then it names a test, such as watching whether a hurt insect avoids a place that hurt her. No one yet knows.
items.why: Neither view can be proved wrong yet. Experiments keep adding evidence, and the question stays open.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Grasshopper, cockroach, dragonfly, ladybird.
items.a: Ladybird. She grows up with a pupa, and the other three grow up in three stages.
items.why: Grasshoppers, cockroaches and dragonflies all have nymphs. A ladybird has a larva and a pupa.

items.p: If a spray is truly needed on a crop that bees visit, which timing harms bees least?
opts: At dusk, after the bees have gone home
At noon, when the flowers are wide open
Any time, because a mild spray never touches a bee
items.why: Bees are out on open flowers at noon, and a spray would land on them. At dusk they are back in the hive. Even then, a mild spray is only for when it is truly needed, and never on open flowers.

worksheets.title: Faulty claims, fair tests and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to spot weak reasoning, plan fair tests and give views on questions with no single answer.

items.p: Zoya sees a caterpillar eating her plant and says, 'Butterflies are pests.' What is wrong?
opts: The caterpillar and the butterfly do different jobs
Caterpillars are never pests
Butterflies eat leaves too
items.why: A caterpillar eats leaves, and the butterfly she becomes carries pollen. One job does not give a name to the whole animal for her whole life.
