items.p: A pupa does nothing, and nothing happens inside her.
items.why: False. Inside the pupa her body is taken apart and rebuilt, and an adult comes out.

items.p: Imagine a beetle as big as a dog. Which problem would she meet first?
opts: Her compound eyes would stop working at that size
She could no longer eat leaves
Air would reach her muscles too slowly, down long tubes
items.why: Insects breathe through air tubes. In a very large body the tubes must be very long, and air creeps slowly down them. Compound eyes and leaf-eating do not depend on size in this way.

items.p: A friend says, 'An insect walking on a hurt leg feels no pain.' Give one reason this does not prove it.
items.a: Hunted animals often hide their weakness, so that a hunter does not see they are hurt. The same sign could have two causes.
items.why: A strong answer says the sign could have another cause, and that we cannot see inside an insect. It does not say insects do feel, only that this sign cannot settle it.

items.p: Dina counts 6 ants at sugar and 2 at salt, once. What should she do before saying, 'Ants love sugar'?
opts: Say it, because 6 is more than 2
Add more salt to the salt
Repeat it, and swap where the foods sit
items.why: One try can be a fluke, and ants may simply like the place nearest to where they arrive. Repeating and swapping the places shows whether the food is the reason.

items.p: Match each young insect to where she lives.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Young insects often live where their food is. A dung beetle grub lives in the dung she eats.

items.p: Sort each case by what people would call the insect there.
items: a termite eating a wooden door
a termite breaking down a fallen log in a forest
a ladybird eating aphids on a rose
a hadda beetle eating brinjal leaves
a lone locust resting in the grass
items.a: as given
items.why: Termites and ladybirds appear in more than one place. The names follow what the insect is doing and what we want.

items.p: A farmer plants marigold and coriander among her vegetables. Which is the best reason?
opts: They poison the aphids
They keep the bees away
They feed hunters such as ladybirds
items.why: Marigold and coriander flowers give hunting insects food and shelter. They do not poison anyone.

items.p: Is 'friend' or 'foe' a fact about an insect, or about us? Use the caterpillar and the butterfly to explain.
items.a: It is about us and our plans. The caterpillar eats the leaf, and the butterfly she becomes carries pollen. It is one insect.
items.why: A strong answer says that the label depends on where the insect is and what we want, and gives the caterpillar example. It may also say that some scientists see the insect's own life as outside friend or foe.

items.p: If every honeybee vanished, many crops would still give some food.
items.why: True. Wild bees, flies and other insects pollinate too, and rice, wheat and maize do not need insects. Some crops would give less, but many would still give food.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding out whether insects are falling in number.
items: Compare the weights from year to year
Set the same traps in the same places
a: Set the same traps in the same places
Compare the weights from year to year
items.why: A fair count uses the same method in the same places for many years. Only then can you compare, and then ask what else changed.

items.p: Scientists disagree about whether insects feel. What would you test, and what result would change your mind?
items.a: Any test with a clear result, such as seeing whether a hurt insect avoids the place where she was hurt. It also needs a clear reason that the result would change the view.
items.why: The answer should give a test, say what the result might be, and say what that would mean. There is no single right test.

items.p: Draw the whole growth of a mosquito. Show which stages live in water.
items.a: Four pictures: an egg on water, a wriggler hanging from the surface, a pupa swimming, then an adult flying away. The first three stages sit in water.
items.why: A mosquito grows up in four stages, and three of them are in still water. That is why still water matters.

items.p: Is it fair to end a silkworm's life to make a sari?

views.who: A weaving family in Kanchipuram (an imagined view)
views.says: Silk gives our family a living. The thread has been woven in our town for generations.
Ending a life to make cloth is harm. Gandhi wrote against ordinary silk.

views.who: Kusuma Rajaiah, a handloom officer from Telangana
views.says: Silk can be made without ending the pupa's life, by letting the moth leave first. This is called ahimsa silk.

items.ask: Which would you choose, and why? What would you want to know first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason. Then it names something still unknown, such as how the cost of ahimsa silk compares, or whether the moth is hurt either way.
items.why: Each view is held by real people. Making silk without ending a life takes more time and costs more, and the question of whether the moth feels stays open.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Ladybird, dragonfly, mantis, dung beetle.
items.a: Dung beetle. The other three hunt other insects, and she clears dung.
items.why: A ladybird, a dragonfly and a mantis are predators. A dung beetle is a decomposer.

items.p: Protecting a crop by helping the insects who hunt the crop's eaters is called ________ control.
items.why: Biological control uses living hunters, such as ladybirds and tiny wasps, instead of poison.

quiz.p: You count eight legs and two body parts on a small creature in a corner. What is she?
opts: An insect with two legs hidden
A young beetle
A spider, not an insect
quiz.why: Eight legs and two body parts make a spider. An insect has six legs and three body parts. If you chose an insect, count the legs again and then the body parts.

quiz.p: A caterpillar has many legs along her body. Is she an insect?
opts: Yes, a young insect with six true legs
No, she has more than six legs
No, only grown-up moths are insects
quiz.why: Only the front six are true legs. The soft ones behind are grips, and a caterpillar is the young stage of an insect. If you said no, you counted the grips as legs.

quiz.p: A male moth finds a female from far away, yet has no nose. What does he smell with?
opts: His compound eyes
His spiracles
His antennae
quiz.why: Antennae carry thousands of sensors for smell. Compound eyes see, and spiracles are breathing holes.

quiz.p: A bee sees ultraviolet lines on a flower that looks plain yellow to you. What does this show?
opts: Bees see light that our eyes cannot
The flower changes colour for the bee
Bees see better than we do in every way
quiz.why: Our eyes and a bee's eyes pick up different light, so the same flower looks different. A compound eye is also less sharp than ours, so bees do not see better in every way.

quiz.p: An ant walks across a ceiling without tipping. Which helps most?
opts: She is too light to fall
Three legs always grip while three move
Her wings hold her up
quiz.why: Her six legs work as two tripods in turn, so three legs always make a steady triangle, with sticky pads and claws to grip. Wings are not used for walking.

quiz.p: A grasshopper nymph has tiny wing buds. What happens to them at each moult?
opts: They fall off
They grow bigger until the wings work
They turn into legs
quiz.why: A nymph looks like a small adult. Each moult makes her bigger, and her wings grow with her. After her last moult the wings work.

quiz.p: Which of these grows up in three stages, with no pupa?
opts: A mosquito
A dragonfly
A ladybird
quiz.why: A dragonfly goes from egg to nymph to adult. A mosquito and a ladybird both go through a pupa, which is four stages.

quiz.p: True or false: a pupa is only resting, and nothing happens inside her.
quiz.why: False. Inside the pupa the body of the larva is taken apart and rebuilt as the adult's body. A pupa often looks still, and a great deal is going on.

quiz.p: A farmer kills every fly in her mango orchard. Mango flowers are mostly pollinated by flies. What is likely?
opts: She will get fewer mangoes
She will get more mangoes
Nothing changes, because wind does the work
quiz.why: Flies carry the pollen from flower to flower, and without pollen a flower cannot make fruit. Wind and self-pollination are how rice and wheat manage, but mango needs its flies.

quiz.p: A gardener watches a bee push into a mustard flower. What does each of them get from this visit?
opts: The bee gets nectar, and the flower's pollen is carried to another flower
The bee gets pollen to eat, and the flower gets nectar
Neither gets anything, because the bee is only resting
quiz.why: The bee drinks the sweet nectar, and the pollen on her body is carried to the next flower, so seeds can grow. Both gain. The bee does not give the flower nectar. The flower makes nectar to pay for the visit.

quiz.p: Ladybirds, dragonflies and tiny wasps help a farmer in the same way. How?
opts: They carry pollen from flower to flower
They hunt insects who eat the crop
They break down dung in the field
quiz.why: All three are hunters, called predators. A farmer who protects them needs less spray. Pollen carriers and dung clearers do other jobs.

quiz.p: A new country's fields fill up with cow pats that do not rot away. What is the likely reason?
opts: Cows make too much dung
No local beetles can handle that dung
Rain washes dung away slowly
quiz.why: Australia found this out. Its dung beetles could not handle cow dung, and the pats covered the pastures until other dung beetles were brought in. Beetles do the clearing work.

quiz.p: A lone locust harms nobody, but a crowd of them ruins crops. What does this show about 'pest'?
opts: Only locusts can be pests
The lone locust is a different animal
The word names what insects do in a place
quiz.why: The lone locust and the swarming locust are the same animal. Crowding changes her colour and behaviour. 'Pest' describes the situation with people, not a kind of insect.

quiz.p: A caterpillar eats a leaf and later pollinates flowers as a butterfly. Which is the fairest thing to say?
opts: She is a pest and stays one
One insect, with two different jobs
She is a pest first and a friend later, so she changed
quiz.why: She is one being doing two jobs at two times in her life. If you chose the last one, notice that she did not change her mind. Only her job changed.

quiz.p: Why can a poison spray leave more aphids on a field than before?
opts: It also kills the ladybirds and wasps who hunted them
Aphids grow bigger on poison
The spray feeds the aphids
quiz.why: A spray reaches every insect that the poison lands on. Aphids breed fastest, so they come back first, with no hunters left to stop them.

quiz.p: Caterpillars are eating young cabbages and bees visit nearby. Which choice is safest for bees?
opts: Cover the young plants with a fine net
Spray at noon, when bees are out
Spray every flower with poison
quiz.why: A net keeps the caterpillars off and does not touch the bees. Spraying at noon or on open flowers reaches the bees.

quiz.p: Bumblebees rolled small wooden balls for no food, and young bees rolled more. What might this suggest?
opts: Bees need balls to build nests
Bees feel exactly as people do
It is hard to explain without something like play
quiz.why: Young mammals play more than old ones too. Some scientists say this hints that bees may feel pleasure, and others say it may be an automatic response. It does not prove bees feel exactly as we do.

quiz.p: A hurt insect keeps walking on a damaged leg. Does this prove she feels no pain?
opts: No, hunted animals often hide weakness
Yes, pain always stops walking
Yes, insects have no nerves
quiz.why: Many hunted animals keep going so that a hunter does not see they are hurt. Insects do have nerve cells. This one sign cannot settle the question.

applications: Engineers build six-legged robots to walk over rubble after an earthquake. They copy the insect's tripod walk, with three legs always on the ground. Search for a video of one climbing over bricks, and notice where its three steady legs are.

In 2008 the papaya mealybug ruined fields in Tamil Nadu, and sprays failed. In 2010 scientists in Bengaluru released a tiny wasp who hunts the mealybug, and the fields recovered. Many farmers also hang small cards carrying the eggs of tiny wasps in sugarcane and other fields, as a way to protect crops without sprays.

Silk saris from Kanchipuram, Mysuru and Assam begin as a caterpillar's thread. Find a silk sari at home and look at its label. Ask where the thread was spun, and by whom, and whether it was mulberry, tussar, eri or muga.

Mosquito nets, a tight lid on the water pot and an empty tray every week all protect people without a spray. Guppy and gambusia fish are put into ponds and wells by many health departments to eat the young mosquitoes. Ask at your local health centre if they give them out.

Beekeepers keep boxes of honeybees at the edge of mustard and sunflower fields, because crops that bees visit often give more seed. Look at a bottle of honey, and notice what is written on its label about where it came from.

Indian farmers have long mixed dried neem leaves into stored grain to keep weevils away, and planted marigold at the edge of vegetable beds. These are bee-safe ways of protecting crops. Ask a grandparent or an older neighbour what they have used in the kitchen or garden.

Gardeners and school gardens can plant flowers on purpose to feed bees and butterflies, such as marigold, tulsi and coriander left to flower. Walk through a park near you and count the flowers a bee could drink from. Notice how many months of the year the park has flowers.

spotted.text: Look at a housefly on a window pane. Notice how her feet hold on to glass, and how she is gone before your hand lands. Her many small eyes catch movement very fast.
spotted.art: A housefly sitting on a window pane with a child's hand about to reach her, drawn close.

spotted.text: After the first rains, look on a tree trunk or a wall for a brown, empty shell with a split down the back. It is the old skin of a cicada or a dragonfly, left behind when she grew. Notice the six legs on the shell.
spotted.art: A brown empty skin clinging to a tree trunk, with a split down the back.

spotted.text: At the vegetable market, look for cabbage, brinjal or drumstick leaves with round holes in them. Notice that somebody has eaten them, and ask what the plant looked like before.
spotted.art: A cabbage leaf with several round holes, held up against the light.

spotted.text: On a tree or weed in flower, watch the flowers for five minutes. Notice who comes: a bee, a fly, a small beetle or a butterfly. Notice whether they touch the middle of the flower.
spotted.art: A tulsi or mango flower with a fly and a small bee, drawn from close.

spotted.text: After a monsoon shower, look at a puddle or a bucket that has stood for a few days. Look for small wrigglers hanging from the surface. Notice how they dive when your shadow falls.
spotted.art: A pot of rainwater with tiny comma-shaped wrigglers hanging from the surface.

spotted.text: At a sari shop, look at the labels on silk saris: mulberry, tussar, eri or muga. Feel the cloth, and ask which place each one comes from. Notice that each name is a different insect or a different tree.
spotted.art: A stack of silk saris with small hand-written labels, and a child's hand on one.

spotted.text: Look under a street lamp after dark in the rains. Notice the moths circling it, and find the wings and the feathery antennae on a moth who has landed on a wall.
spotted.art: A street lamp at dusk with moths circling, and one moth on a wall below.

spotted.text: On a village path or park after rain, look for a dung beetle rolling a ball. Notice how she keeps going in a straight line, even when the ball is bigger than she is.
spotted.art: A dung beetle rolling a round ball along a dusty path, with her back legs pushing.

ask_kids: How many legs does an insect have, and where do they join her body? Can you check on the next insect you see?
A caterpillar and a butterfly are the same animal at two times of her life. Which would you rather be for a day, and why?
Which insect have you seen today? What was she doing? Would you call her a friend, a foe or both, and what made you choose?
A bee sees colours that you cannot see. What do you think a flower looks like to her?
If you could ask an ant one question, what would you ask? How could you find out the answer without asking her?
Where does the water stand still near your home? What could you do about it this week?
Silk comes from a caterpillar's thread. Is it fair to use it? What would you want to know before deciding?
Do you think an insect can feel? What have you seen an insect do that makes you think so, or not?

jokes.j: Why could the spider not join the insect club?
jokes.a: She had two legs too many and one body part too few.

jokes.j: What did the ant say when you wiped away her smell trail?
A dragonfly's teacher said, 'Keep your eyes on your own paper.' What did the dragonfly say?
Why do bees have sticky hair?
Why was the silkworm the best at telling long stories?
jokes.a: She could spin a thread for a kilometre without stopping.

jokes.j: What did the caterpillar say to her friends before she went into the cocoon?
jokes.a: 'See you later. I have some changes to make.'

jokes.j: What did the dung beetle say when she found a perfect ball of dung?
jokes.a: 'This is my lucky day. I will just roll with it.'

jokes.j: Why did the quiet locust get a bad name?
jokes.a: She started hanging out with the wrong crowd.

jokes.j: Why was the pupa late for school?
What do you call a bee who cannot make up her mind?
Why did the bee get married?
What did the tree say to the woodpecker?

maths.problem: A silkworm grows to about ten thousand times her first weight in four weeks. A baby weighs 3 kilograms at birth. How heavy would the baby be if she grew ten thousand times?
maths.explain: 3 × 10,000 = 30,000. A baby growing that fast would weigh about as much as six elephants. A silkworm does it in a month because she is so tiny at the start.
maths.context: This problem scales a silkworm's growth up to the size of a baby.
maths.why_maths: Growth by a number of times is multiplication, and it shows how large the change from egg to full-grown silkworm really is.

maths.problem: A cockroach runs about 50 of her own body lengths every second. Her body is 4 centimetres long. How fast is she in centimetres per second? If a person who is 1.5 metres tall ran 50 body lengths a second, how many metres per second would that be?
maths.answer: 200 centimetres per second, which is 2 metres per second. The person would run 75 metres per second.
maths.explain: 50 × 4 = 200 centimetres. A person: 50 × 1.5 = 75 metres per second, which is much faster than the fastest sprinter at about 10 metres per second.
maths.context: This problem compares the speed of a small animal and a large one by body length.
maths.why_maths: Comparing by body length is a ratio. It shows why a small animal can be fast for her size, even if her speed is small.

maths.problem: For one kind of honeybee, a waggle lasting 1 second shows food about 1 kilometre away. A dancing bee waggles for 3 seconds, and another for 5 seconds. How far is each patch of flowers? How much farther is the second?
maths.answer: 3 kilometres and 5 kilometres. The second is 2 kilometres farther.
maths.explain: The waggle time is the distance in kilometres, so 3 seconds means 3 kilometres and 5 seconds means 5. 5 − 3 = 2.
maths.context: This problem uses the waggle rule as a number rule.
maths.why_maths: A rule that turns one number into another is an input and output rule. Bees use such a rule without writing it down.

maths.problem: Mosquito young need about 8 days in water to become adults. A family empties the water tray every 7 days. Another empties it every 10 days. Which family stops the young becoming adults? Why?
maths.answer: The family who empties every 7 days. Eggs laid on day 1 have only 7 days before the water goes, which is less than 8.
maths.explain: Compare 7 with 8 and 10. If the time between emptyings is shorter than the time the young need, none can finish growing. A gap of 10 days is longer than 8, so some can.
maths.context: This problem compares two weekly routines with the time a mosquito needs to grow up.
maths.why_maths: Deciding whether a routine works means comparing two times. This is the same thinking that health workers use in setting up checks.

maths.problem: Scientists estimate about 25 lakh ants for every person on Earth. How many ants is that for a family of 4? Write it in lakhs and in crores.
maths.context: This problem uses the ant estimate to practise big numbers in the Indian system.
maths.why_maths: To picture a huge number of ants you need to move between lakhs and crores. The same step is how we read big numbers in newspapers.

maths.problem: A desert locust swarm covering 1 square kilometre eats in a day what about 35,000 people eat. Suppose a swarm in India covers 5 square kilometres. How many people's food would it eat in one day?
maths.explain: 35,000 × 5 = 1,75,000. If the swarm stays 3 days, multiply by 3 again: 5,25,000.
maths.context: This problem multiplies the daily food of a swarm by its size.
maths.why_maths: The size of a swarm is judged by multiplying a small amount by a large area. This is how scientists tell farmers how much to worry.

warmup.q: How many legs does a grown-up insect have, and how many parts has her body?
warmup.a: Six legs, in three pairs, and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

warmup.q: A creature has eight legs and two body parts. Is she an insect?
warmup.a: No. She is a spider, who has eight legs and two body parts.

warmup.q: What does an insect do when her skin becomes too small?
warmup.a: She sheds it and grows a bigger one. This is called moulting.

warmup.q: Which grows up with a pupa: a silk moth or a grasshopper?
warmup.a: The silk moth. A grasshopper goes from egg to nymph to adult, with no pupa.

warmup.q: What does a bee carry from flower to flower?
warmup.a: Pollen. This is called pollination, and it lets a flower make seeds and fruit.

warmup.q: Name two insects who hunt other insects.
warmup.a: A ladybird, a dragonfly, a praying mantis, a lacewing or a tiny wasp, among others.
Only females bite. They need the protein in blood to make their eggs.

warmup.q: A caterpillar eats your plant. What does she become?
warmup.a: A moth or a butterfly. She may then carry pollen from flower to flower.

quiz: A spider is an insect.
Insects have six legs and three body parts, and spiders have eight legs.
An insect's skeleton is on the outside.
It is called an exoskeleton, and the insect sheds this cover to grow.
A silk moth grows up with a pupa stage.
She goes from egg to silkworm to pupa to moth.
Bees see red as bright red.
Bees do not see red well. They do see ultraviolet, which we cannot see.
Only female mosquitoes bite.
Females need blood to make their eggs. Males drink nectar.
A caterpillar has more than six true legs.
She has six true legs at the front. The soft ones behind are grips.
All bees live in hives.
A carpenter bee nests alone in a hole in wood.
Rice needs insects to carry its pollen.
Rice does not need insects. Its pollen stays in its own flower or travels on the wind.
A locust is always a swarming insect.
A lone locust lives alone. Crowding changes her into the swarming kind.
Ladybirds only eat aphids.
Some, like the hadda beetle, eat brinjal and potato leaves.
odd: The other three are insects. A spider is not.
A nymph belongs to the three-stage life. The other three are stages of a four-stage life.
The first three hunt other insects. A dung beetle clears dung.
The first three are silks from insects. Cotton comes from a plant.
The other three are the body's parts. Antennae are on the head.
